ingredients.name: Strategy-tree walk (first-player coverage)
ingredients.what: Each relabelled iteration walks the net's own first-player tree (its raw move at its positions, every reply at the opponent's) and relabels those positions with the net's own search. The targeted coverage for perfect play from the start (P-START).
ingredients.conclusion: Works, and replaces the siblings for the P-START goal: perfect first-player play on 10/10 tic-tac-toe seeds with siblings off (h73), and on Connect-4 an iteration dropped from 4,008 s to 32 s together with parallel relabelling (h77).

ingredients.name: Solver-free stop signal
ingredients.what: Stop training when, on the net's own first-player tree, every raw move agrees with the net's own search (zero disagreements).
ingredients.conclusion: Safe and timely on tic-tac-toe with siblings (h69) and without (h74): 0 false stops, latency 0-1 iterations. On Connect-4 it never fires (h88). Most disagreements there are harmless — both moves optimal (59%) — or the search's fault (16%) (h90), but none of the nets is certified through 10 plies (h91) and at the first failing ply the net and its 200-sim search mostly agree on the losing move (h92): an agreement signal cannot be made safe on Connect-4 until the opening labels are right. Counting equal-value moves as agreement does not rescue it. A value-aware reading (a move also agrees within search Q 0.1 of the top move) passed the tic-tac-toe recalibration (h101), but only vacuously: it never differed from the share reading there (h102). On the six T10 Connect-4 nets it also equals the share reading at delta 0.05 and 0.1, and delta 0.2 removes at most 21% (h103, h105): the search itself values the rejected moves more than 0.1 lower, so the share rule already is a value rule. The value head is part of the cause but not all of it: it backs 42% of the nets' wrong moves (h106, inconclusive between the 40% and 60% bars), 57% at plies 0-4, and at the empty board every value head rates the winning centre below at least two other moves (h107). The rest are policy-side, where the value head ranks the right move higher one move ahead — yet the net's own 200-sim search labels an optimal move there only 47% of the time (h108, inconclusive), 15% at plies 2-4, and only 18% where the value head backs the error (h109). In the opening the training target itself is wrong at most of the nets' errors, so the value signal the search reads, not how the policy fits its labels, is the lever.

ingredients.name: Siblings (one- and two-move deviations)
ingredients.what: Relabel every position one (or two) moves away from the recorded self-play positions along moves self-play did not take.
ingredients.conclusion: Work on tic-tac-toe: one-ply siblings cut raw failures, mostly in-sample (h31, h38); two-deep siblings with augmentation gave raw-perfect nets on 10/10 seeds (h52), the remaining failures sitting on untrained positions (h57). Without augmentation they fail (h54, h55). They do not scale to Connect-4 (over 90% of an iteration, h76) and are replaced there by the strategy tree.

ingredients.name: Symmetry augmentation
ingredients.what: Train on every symmetric image of each example, with each game's symmetries found and verified rather than assumed.
ingredients.conclusion: Necessary in the tic-tac-toe process: every arm without it failed (h46, h50, h54, h55, h56), and augmentation with two-deep siblings gave 10/10 (h52). Convergence alone was not enough (h45). Symmetries are found by proof per game (t20).

ingredients.name: Standardised (canonical) input
ingredients.what: Map each position to its smallest-key symmetric image before the net sees it, so the net never has to learn the symmetry.
ingredients.conclusion: Shrinks what a net must represent (a 938-param net holds perfect tic-tac-toe when fitted to the answers, h51), but the solver-free process could not reach it at about 1K params, even with the final training pass matched to the oracle fit's budget (h58, h59, h60, h63, h64, h65).

ingredients.name: Relabelling with a deeper search (reanalyse)
ingredients.what: Relabel the whole buffer each iteration with a 200-sim search of the current net.
ingredients.conclusion: Works and replicates on tic-tac-toe, through the policy prior (h25, h26, h34, h35, h36, h37), but is a partial cause of the fix, not the whole of it (h28). On Connect-4 a 200-sim relabel search is silently wrong in the opening (h92), and more search does not fix it: 200 / 2,000 / 20,000 sims are right at 86.5 / 87.2 / 83.7% of opening positions and at only 33-60% of the first moves, 56% at 100,000 (h96; h93 inconclusive by its bars). The search reads the value head, so the value signal is the lever (stop_signal, h106-h109): value targets for the strategy-tree positions, from the relabel search's root value, do no harm on tic-tac-toe (h110: 10/10 seeds still perfect from the start, stop still safe). On Connect-4 neither they nor n-step bootstrapped value targets help: in a paired 4-seed pilot the share of optimal moves at the nets' own opening positions fell from 86% to 82% and 75% (h111, h112, both refuted). Both targets come from the net itself, and the readout shows the echo: with search-value targets the value head backs 73% of the opening errors, against 36% without (h113). A value target the net computes cannot add information it lacks; it has to come from real game outcomes. The backward curriculum (games started near the end, moving back) is the first such fix; it does no harm on tic-tac-toe (h114: 10/10 seeds still perfect from the start, stop safe), but in a paired 4-seed Connect-4 pilot it did not raise the share of optimal opening moves (72% vs 73%, 1 win of 4; h115 refuted). That pilot measure is noisy: the unchanged process scores 86% and 73% on two sets of four seeds, and single nets range from 62% to 94% (h116), so the three refutations rule out large gains only. The next pilot must be powered first. Scored on one fixed set of 5,142 exactly valued positions instead, nets of one arm spread 3.5 points and seed-matched differences 3.1, so 7 seed pairs detect a 3-point gain and 16 a 2-point one (h117); post hoc on that set all three refuted treatments read 1.7-2.1 points above base, a hypothesis that the powered pre-registered run (four arms, seven fresh seeds, Holm-corrected permutation tests) mostly did not reproduce: tree values -0.4 and the curriculum -2.3 points (h119, h120 refuted); only n-step kept its direction, +3.4 points on 5 of 7 pairs, uncorrected p 0.031, short of Holm's bar (h118 inconclusive; h121). No net in any arm is certified through 6 plies. Next real-outcome fix: an exploiter in self-play (the current net with 8x search, greedy, in half the games); its first tic-tac-toe no-harm run could not be judged because the run recorder missed the exploiter games (h122 not run; dead end h123, fixed); rerun on fresh seeds it does no harm (h124: 10/10 seeds still perfect from the start, stop safe); but on Connect-4 it changed nothing: +0.06 points on the fixed set (p 0.48; h125 inconclusive) and 71.1% vs 71.2% optimal at plies 0-4 (h126), though it played ~470 games per seed. Of the five fixes tried, only n-step shows a lead, and none makes the opening right (0 certified nets in every arm). Running the base process three times as long settles why: from iteration 20 to 60 general play keeps improving (+5.5 points on the fixed set, h128) but the opening does not move (+0.5 points at plies 0-4, h127 refuted; one seed fell from 75% to 68%). The opening is not waiting on a longer run — this self-play process does not learn it at this scale, whatever the value-signal fix. The hybrid's first measurement: an exact opening exception table computed by the process, with the net carrying the next ply, certifies on none of the ten nets at any horizon (h129, h130 refuted). The table overrides 50%, 26% and 15% of its positions before plies 3, 5 and 7, and the net is wrong at 23%, 12% and 12% of the ply it carries (h131): it improves with depth but its tree grows ~6x per ply. A hybrid certified through 10 would need ~190 table entries per net (~12% of its first-player positions). Training the net beside the table works: with self-play started at the table's frontier and the strategy tree walked from there, the net plays the optimal move at 81.6% of the 284 positions one ply past the table against 75.0% for the base process (+6.5 points, 6 of 7 seed pairs, p 0.016; h132 supported) and fails less at the never-trained ply 8 too (681 vs 865; h133). No hybrid certifies through 9 plies yet. Training the net on both plies it carries (6 and 8) from the frontier (H3) could not be judged: it was launched with 6 relabel workers against the registered 4 (h138; h134, h135 inconclusive by protocol). With the run's own worker count the registered tests are still inconclusive — +1.2 points at ply 8 (5 of 7, p 0.14) and a ply-6 curve that has flattened (+0.6 points over the last ten passes, most of the gain by pass 10; h139). H3 needs fewer table exceptions on 6 of 7 seeds (253 vs 278 entries; h141), but every certified-through-9 hybrid is over 25x the size of a table alone over the same tree: the 20,616-parameter net at 32 bits dominates, and break-even is about 1 bit per weight (h140). Through ply 9 the smallest certified description is the table.

ingredients.name: Unique buffer and final settle
ingredients.what: Keep each position once in the buffer and finish with a long, low-rate training pass (the settle).
ingredients.conclusion: Helps, not sufficient alone: with augmentation it was inconclusive (h49); a 1,500-epoch settle made the 5,008-param residual net raw-perfect where 30 epochs did not (h62 vs h61); it did not rescue the 1K standardised-input nets (h59, h60).

ingredients.name: Random openings
ingredients.what: Start self-play games after random opening moves to widen what self-play visits.
ingredients.conclusion: Does not work: mixed openings raised visits to the starved positions 4.5x without fixing them (h19, h20, h21, h23), so starvation is a correlate, not the cause (h22); six random opening moves failed in T5 with and without augmentation (h53, h56).

ingredients.name: Self-play search depth
ingredients.what: How many simulations the self-play search spends per move.
ingredients.conclusion: At matched compute shallow search first looked better (h3), but the effect decayed and reversed at full convergence: deeper search plateaus higher (h8). Part of the early gap was a deployment-budget confound (h9 holds at a neutral budget, h10 is null at the shallow arm's own). Deeper self-play alone did not fix the tic-tac-toe blind spot (h27), a failure of that recipe rather than of labels (h29).

ingredients.name: Exact solver labels
ingredients.what: Train on the solver's exact best moves instead of search labels (an oracle, not solver-free).
ingredients.conclusion: Without siblings, exact labels were the worst residual arm (h40): exact answers on the wrong positions do not give coverage.

ingredients.name: Net size and the smallest-net frontier
ingredients.what: How small a net can hold perfect play, and how the frontier is searched (oracle fits, strategy fits, bisection with checks above).
ingredients.conclusion: Tic-tac-toe: about 5K params hold perfect play (h47) and the process reaches it at 5,008 (h62). Connect-4 first-player play: 1,576 params certified through 8 plies (h67) and 20,616 through 10, with 8,008 unable to hold its data at 10 (h68, h72): roughly x5-13 per two plies. A 335K net trained earlier fails at its second move (h66).

ingredients.name: P-START certification
ingredients.what: The solver walks the net's own first-player tree against every reply and checks every move keeps the proven value (staged by depth).
ingredients.conclusion: Works as a staged certificate. The root value is taken as the theorem it is instead of solved (h78), the native solver's table bug is guarded (h79), and certified nets are now saved and independently re-checked (h87).

ingredients.name: Solver-free guarantee and parallel relabelling
ingredients.what: Proof that training called no solver, and the relabel search spread over worker processes bit-identically.
ingredients.conclusion: The unchanged process learned Othello with no solver (h1). The guard covers the Python and the native solver since h86. Parallel relabelling is part of the ~125x Connect-4 speed-up (h77); its result handoff no longer uses torch shared memory and a silent pool now raises (h89). DECISION 2026-10-02 (user): brute force (bigger nets, days of compute) and rules supplied from outside the process are ruled out. Self-play itself is NOT rejected: at our budget it plateaus wrong in the opening, 100x more labelling search, written certificates and a value-aware stop did not fix it (see stop_signal, search_budget, written_rules), and net size is not the limit (net_size), so the training method itself is the next suspect — first the value head's training signal.

ingredients.name: Written rules (§C.50)
ingredients.what: Play knowledge as logical statements (decision lists over predicates), verified exactly by the solver and fed to the other agents.
ingredients.conclusion: Win, block and fork are position-sound, and settle 89% of tic-tac-toe and 29% of the Connect-4 positions our nets visit (h70). Newell–Simon is a perfect strategy from the start for both sides but is not position-sound (h71). With only the 11 current predicates no position-sound playbook exists up to 12 rules (h94, pre-registered, refuted) or even 60 (h95): the obstruction is across positions, so the language needs richer predicates, not more rules. Adding three layered forced-outcome predicates (wins_in_5, gives_loss_in_4, gives_loss_in_6) makes a 3-rule, 3-literal playbook position-sound at all 4,520 positions, proven minimal by SAT (h97) — the knowledge moves into the predicates, whose lookahead (up to 6 plies) is the price. On Connect-4, Allis-style value certificates (a claimeven/baseinverse pairing for Black) never contradict the solver (h98), but they cannot supply the opening: none of the search's 144 wrong opening moves is flagged (h99, pre-registered, refuted). Through ply 8 of the nets' trees no position is certified, and certificates flag 0.5% of non-winning moves beyond the immediate-win tactic. They are an endgame tool, certifying 2 to 43 of 150 random positions as stones go from 20 to 38+ (h100).

ingredients.name: Diagnosing failures (the tic-tac-toe blind spot)
ingredients.what: Where and why the nets fail: localisation, replication, starvation, the metric itself.
ingredients.conclusion: The blind spot is systematic and replicates (h11, h18, h24), is not explained by the eval budget (h12) or off-manifold enrichment (h14, h16), and self-play never trains the positions involved (h30). The coverage metric was wrong until it read every orientation (h39). Connect-4 accuracy away from training data is data-limited (h48).

ingredients.name: Training budget and game generality
ingredients.what: More games on the unchanged process, and new games without harness changes.
ingredients.conclusion: Returns past ~9,600 Othello games are unresolved (h2); the deeper-search arm was still improving at 28,800 games (h7). New games need zero harness changes (t7, t8). Kalah, the next ladder rung, plugs in as one file and matches the published solution (Irving, Donkers & Uiterwijk 2000) on every shape solved (h136); the paper's perfect games fit its stated rules best, its 4(6) line is misprinted (h137). But Kalah's extra move is the first rule that keeps the same mover, and the certifier and the search's proof step negate every child's value (strict xfails in tests/test_alternation.py) — Checkers avoided it by folding a multi-jump into one turn (t7).

ingredients.name: Measurement integrity
ingredients.what: Resume, eras and fingerprints, the register, the statistics, mutation testing: the guards that keep results honest.
ingredients.conclusion: Each guard exists because an earlier reading was wrong without it, and each is a supported, test-backed claim; the two latest dead ends were a register hook that applied one arm's outcome to every arm (h82) and a hand-run mutation hidden by stale bytecode (h83).

unproven_trials.what: The first Connect-4 depth-12 strategy run was replaced, with the user's agreement, by depth 10 with larger nets.
unproven_trials.lesson: Depth 12 costs days per width on this machine; get the depth-10 bracket first.

unproven_trials.what: The first depth-10 strategy run was stopped and restarted.
unproven_trials.lesson: Refits must warm-start and the label cache must be saved atomically after every batch, or a stopped run loses hours of solves.

unproven_trials.what: My mid-run reading of the depth-10 failures as loop instability was wrong.
unproven_trials.lesson: Read whether each refit held its data before blaming the loop (corrected in h68).

unproven_trials.what: An existing Connect-4 solver library (BitBully) was considered and rejected for its AGPL licence.
unproven_trials.lesson: Write our own solver (harness/c4solver.c, a port of harness/solver.py); the provenance of solver.py is still open.

unproven_trials.what: The C solver source could not join the code fingerprint, which parses Python only.
unproven_trials.lesson: The compiled library is named by the hash of its source, so an edited solver is always rebuilt and identifiable.

unproven_trials.what: A proof module was added to the evidence guard before its evidence existed, failing the suite.
unproven_trials.lesson: Add a proof module to the guard only once its data file is recorded.

unproven_trials.what: Changes to fingerprinted training code were needed while a long run was active.
unproven_trials.lesson: Work in a scratch copy and copy back after the run exits, merging the register and the evidence manifest rather than overwriting them.

unproven_trials.what: The first Connect-4 solver-free pilot (2-deep siblings) was abandoned after one iteration.
unproven_trials.lesson: Time one iteration before registering a long run (h76 records the numbers).

unproven_trials.what: Mutation specs and pilot data were kept in a temporary folder, and one spec was overwritten.
unproven_trials.lesson: Specs live in tests/mutations/ with their last run; pilot data goes to evidence/ and the register.
